Maximum a Posteriori (MAP)

Combine a likelihood with a prior and compare posterior modes with maximum-likelihood estimates.

Posterior and MAP Objective

Combine Observed Data And Prior Information

Maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation gives a point estimate of an unknown parameter using observed data and a prior distribution over that parameter. It is closely related to maximum likelihood estimation (MLE), but augments the optimization objective with the prior density.

Model
A likelihood \(p(D\mid\theta)\) together with a prior \(p(\theta)\). The coin example uses Bernoulli observations and a beta prior; the regularization section uses priors on model coefficients.
Parameters to estimate
The unknown model parameters \(\theta\), or coefficient vector \(\boldsymbol\beta\) in the regularization examples. Prior means, variances, scales, and beta hyperparameters are treated as fixed here.

The MAP estimate is a mode of the posterior density: it is a parameter value at which that density is maximized.

Suppose we want to estimate a parameter \(\theta\) from observed data \(D\). Bayes’ rule gives:

\[p(\theta\mid D)=\frac{p(D\mid\theta)p(\theta)}{p(D)}\]
TermMeaning
\(\displaystyle p(D\mid\theta)\)Likelihood: the probability mass or density of the observed data as a function of the parameter.
\(\displaystyle p(\theta)\)Prior: the parameter distribution before observing these data.
\(\displaystyle p(\theta\mid D)\)Posterior: the parameter distribution after incorporating the observed data.
\(\displaystyle p(D)\)Evidence: the normalizing term, independent of the parameter being optimized.

MAP combines the log-likelihood with the log-prior. The prior term gives MAP its connection to regularization.

Full derivation: Complete mathematical derivation ↓

Comparison with MLE

Likelihood And Posterior Maximization

MAP combines MLE with prior information. The two methods answer related questions:

MethodInterpretationObjective
Maximum Likelihood EstimationWhich parameter makes the observed data most likely?
\[\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}=\underset{\theta}{\operatorname{arg\,max}}\;p(D\mid\theta)\]

Earlier derivations: Maximum likelihood and score equations

Maximum A Posteriori EstimationWhich parameter has the highest posterior density, given both the data and the prior information?
\[\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MAP}}=\underset{\theta}{\operatorname{arg\,max}}\;p(D\mid\theta)p(\theta)\]

Compared with MLE, MAP favors values supported by the prior. The influence of a fixed prior is typically more noticeable with fewer observations.

If the prior density is constant over the same parameter domain used for MLE, MAP and MLE have the same maximizers. A uniform prior on a restricted interval instead gives the MLE constrained to that interval.

MLE is an argmax of the likelihood or log-likelihood. MAP is an argmax of the posterior. The likelihood is an objective function, not a probability distribution over \(\theta\). The term mode refers to a probability density or mass function, so it directly applies to the posterior used by MAP.

Coin-Flip Example

Example

Eight Heads In Ten Flips

Model
10 independent Bernoulli flips with head probability \(\theta\). MAP additionally uses the fixed prior \(\theta\sim\operatorname{Beta}(2,2)\).
Parameters to estimate
The head probability \(\theta\in(0,1)\). Compare its MLE and MAP estimates; the prior hyperparameters 2 and 2 are fixed.

A coin has an unknown probability of heads \(P(H)=\theta\). Flip it independently 10 times and observe 8 heads and 2 tails.

QuantityCalculation
01

Likelihood

\[p(D\mid\theta)\propto\theta^8(1-\theta)^2\]
02

MLE Point Estimate

\[\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}=\frac{8}{10}=0.8\]
03

Prior

\[\theta\sim\operatorname{Beta}(2,2)\]
\[p(\theta)\propto\theta^1(1-\theta)^1,\qquad 0<\theta<1\]

The likelihood is unchanged. For MAP, multiply it by the prior to obtain the posterior up to a normalizing constant:

Derivation Combine The Likelihood And Prior
\(\displaystyle p(\theta\mid D)\)
\(\propto\)\(\displaystyle \theta^8(1-\theta)^2\,\theta^1(1-\theta)^1\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \theta^9(1-\theta)^3\)

This is the kernel of a beta posterior:

\[\theta\mid D\sim\operatorname{Beta}(10,4)\]

For a \(\operatorname{Beta}(a,b)\) distribution with \(a>1\) and \(b>1\), the mode is \(\frac{a-1}{a+b-2}\). Therefore:

\(\displaystyle \hat\theta_{\mathrm{MAP}}\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{10-1}{10+4-2}\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{9}{12}=0.75\)
\[\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}=0.8,\qquad\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MAP}}=0.75\]

The \(\operatorname{Beta}(2,2)\) prior favors values near \(0.5\), pulling the MAP estimate toward \(0.5\) relative to the MLE.

Priors and Regularization

The Prior As A Penalty

The likelihood measures fit to observed data; the prior encodes plausibility before seeing them. MAP balances both. A parameter with low prior density must fit the data sufficiently better to compensate.

For a coefficient vector \(\boldsymbol\beta=(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_d)\), define the data-fitting loss as the total negative log-likelihood:

\[\mathcal L(\boldsymbol\beta)=-\log p(D\mid\boldsymbol\beta)\]
\[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\mathrm{MAP}}=\underset{\boldsymbol\beta}{\operatorname{arg\,min}}\;\left[\mathcal L(\boldsymbol\beta)-\log p(\boldsymbol\beta)\right]\]

The term \(-\log p(\boldsymbol\beta)\) is the regularizer. With the prior hyperparameters fixed, any additive term that does not depend on \(\boldsymbol\beta\) can be removed without changing the minimizer. Below, \(C\) denotes such a constant.

For priors centered at zero, this favors smaller coefficient magnitudes. The estimate balances fit to the data against the penalty; the coefficients are still estimated from the data.

Gaussian Prior: Why It Gives L2

Assume independent Gaussian priors on the coefficients, all centered at zero and all with the same variance \(\tau^2>0\):

\[\beta_j\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau^2),\qquad j=1,\ldots,d\]

The density for one coefficient is:

\[p(\beta_j)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\tau^2}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\beta_j^2}{2\tau^2}\right)\]

The squared coefficient already appears in the exponent. Taking a negative logarithm removes the exponential and leaves a quadratic penalty. Independence makes the joint prior a product, so its negative logarithm is a sum:

\[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\mathrm{MAP}}=\underset{\boldsymbol\beta}{\operatorname{arg\,min}}\;\left[\mathcal L(\boldsymbol\beta)+\lambda\|\boldsymbol\beta\|_2^2\right]\]
Full derivation: Derivation Negative Log Of A Gaussian Prior ↓
\[\lambda=\frac{1}{2\tau^2},\qquad\|\boldsymbol\beta\|_2^2=\sum_{j=1}^{d}\beta_j^2\]

This is L2 regularization, using the squared L2 norm. A narrower Gaussian prior means smaller \(\tau^2\), a larger penalty weight \(\lambda\), and stronger pressure toward zero.

Laplace Prior: Why It Gives L1

Assume independent Laplace priors on the coefficients, all centered at zero and all with the same scale \(b>0\):

\[\beta_j\sim\operatorname{Laplace}(0,b),\qquad j=1,\ldots,d\]

The density for one coefficient is:

\[p(\beta_j)=\frac{1}{2b}\exp\!\left(-\frac{|\beta_j|}{b}\right)\]

Here the exponent contains the absolute value of the coefficient. Taking a negative logarithm therefore gives an absolute-value penalty:

\[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\mathrm{MAP}}=\underset{\boldsymbol\beta}{\operatorname{arg\,min}}\;\left[\mathcal L(\boldsymbol\beta)+\lambda\|\boldsymbol\beta\|_1\right]\]
Full derivation: Derivation Negative Log Of A Laplace Prior ↓
\[\lambda=\frac{1}{b},\qquad\|\boldsymbol\beta\|_1=\sum_{j=1}^{d}|\beta_j|\]

This is L1 regularization. A smaller Laplace scale \(b\) gives a narrower prior, a larger penalty weight \(\lambda\), and stronger pressure toward zero.

The L2 penalty is smooth and grows quadratically with coefficient magnitude. The L1 penalty grows linearly and has a corner at zero, which can make some estimated coefficients exactly zero. L2 typically shrinks coefficients without making them exactly zero.

Common Spread And The Prior Mean

Common means shared across the coefficients. A common variance uses one value of \(\tau^2\) for every Gaussian prior; a common scale uses one value of \(b\) for every Laplace prior. The coefficients can still take different values. Independence is a separate assumption, used above to multiply their prior densities.

PropertyGaussian PriorLaplace Prior
Shared Spread Parameter
\[\tau_1^2=\cdots=\tau_d^2=\tau^2\]
\[b_1=\cdots=b_d=b\]
Variance Of Each Coefficient
\[\operatorname{Var}(\beta_j)=\tau^2\]
\[\operatorname{Var}(\beta_j)=2b^2\]
Standard Deviation
\[\operatorname{SD}(\beta_j)=\tau\]
\[\operatorname{SD}(\beta_j)=\sqrt{2}\,b\]
Shared Penalty Weight
\[\lambda=\frac{1}{2\tau^2}\]
\[\lambda=\frac{1}{b}\]

The Laplace scale \(b\) controls the width of the distribution; it is neither its variance nor its standard deviation. In both models, a smaller spread means stronger regularization, and a larger spread allows larger departures from the prior center.

A common spread gives every coefficient the same penalty weight in the chosen coefficient units. If coefficients have different prior spreads, the penalties become weighted:

PriorPenalty With Coefficient-Specific Spreads
Independent Gaussian Priors
\[\sum_{j=1}^{d}\frac{\beta_j^2}{2\tau_j^2}\]
Independent Laplace Priors
\[\sum_{j=1}^{d}\frac{|\beta_j|}{b_j}\]

Coefficients with narrower priors are penalized more strongly. Comparing equal penalty weights across coefficients also depends on the units of the predictors; standardizing predictors makes their coefficient magnitudes easier to compare.

The prior mean sets the shrinkage target. Zero-centered priors favor coefficients near zero. If the prior for coefficient \(\beta_j\) is instead centered at a specified mean \(m_j\), the penalty measures departure from that mean:

Prior Centered At \(\displaystyle m_j\)Penalty
\[\beta_j\sim\mathcal N(m_j,\tau^2)\]
\[\frac{1}{2\tau^2}\sum_{j=1}^{d}(\beta_j-m_j)^2\]
\[\beta_j\sim\operatorname{Laplace}(m_j,b)\]
\[\frac{1}{b}\sum_{j=1}^{d}|\beta_j-m_j|\]

The prior center specifies which coefficient values are favored, the prior spread controls how strongly departures are penalized, and the prior shape determines whether the penalty is quadratic, absolute-value, or another form.

The formulas for \(\lambda\) above use the total negative log-likelihood \(\mathcal L\). If the loss is averaged over observations or multiplied by another constant, the penalty weight must be rescaled with it to represent the same prior.

Limitations

A Point Estimate Of The Posterior

MAP is a point estimate, so it does not by itself describe posterior uncertainty. It does not represent Bayesian inference as a whole, which uses probability distributions to summarize information and draw inferences.

Bayesian summaries can instead report the posterior mean or median, together with credible intervals and other features of the posterior distribution.

Derivations and full mathematical details

All original proofs and intermediate calculations are retained below. The links in the sections above lead here.

From: Posterior And MAP Objective ↑

From Bayes’ Rule To The MAP Objective

Choose the parameter value that maximizes the posterior. The evidence \(p(D)\) does not depend on \(\theta\), so it can be omitted from the maximization. Taking logarithms preserves the maximizer and turns the product into a sum:

\(\displaystyle \hat\theta_{\mathrm{MAP}}\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \underset{\theta}{\operatorname{arg\,max}}\;p(\theta\mid D)\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \underset{\theta}{\operatorname{arg\,max}}\;p(D\mid\theta)p(\theta)\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \underset{\theta}{\operatorname{arg\,max}}\;\left[\log p(D\mid\theta)+\log p(\theta)\right]\)
From: Priors And Regularization ↑
Derivation Negative Log Of A Gaussian Prior
\[p(\boldsymbol\beta)=\prod_{j=1}^{d}p(\beta_j)\]
\(\displaystyle -\log p(\boldsymbol\beta)\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle -\sum_{j=1}^{d}\log p(\beta_j)\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^{d}\left[\frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi\tau^2)+\frac{\beta_j^2}{2\tau^2}\right]\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{d}{2}\log(2\pi\tau^2)+\frac{1}{2\tau^2}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\beta_j^2\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle C+\frac{1}{2\tau^2}\|\boldsymbol\beta\|_2^2\)
From: Priors And Regularization ↑
Derivation Negative Log Of A Laplace Prior
\[p(\boldsymbol\beta)=\prod_{j=1}^{d}p(\beta_j)\]
\(\displaystyle -\log p(\boldsymbol\beta)\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle -\sum_{j=1}^{d}\log p(\beta_j)\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^{d}\left[\log(2b)+\frac{|\beta_j|}{b}\right]\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle d\log(2b)+\frac{1}{b}\sum_{j=1}^{d}|\beta_j|\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle C+\frac{1}{b}\|\boldsymbol\beta\|_1\)

Normal–Normal conjugacy as precision-weighted estimation — mathematical details

Multiply the prior \(\exp[-(\mu-\mu_0)^2/(2\tau_0^2)]\) by the Normal likelihood \(\exp[-\sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)]\).

Group terms in \(\mu\): the quadratic coefficient is \(\tau_0^{-2}+n\sigma^{-2}\), and the linear coefficient is \(\mu_0/\tau_0^2+n\bar x/\sigma^2\). Completing the square identifies the posterior precision and mean shown above.

Expectation Maximization (EM)

Use latent-variable responsibilities and alternating optimization to fit models with missing component labels.

Latent Variables and the EM Idea

Estimate Parameters With Unobserved Variables

Expectation maximization (EM) iteratively estimates model parameters with unobserved latent variables. It uses a more manageable complete-data model to optimize an MLE objective, or MAP when a prior is included.

Model
A latent-variable model \(p(X,Z\mid\theta)\). The worked model is a mixture of a specified number \(K\) of Gaussian components.
Parameters to estimate
The model parameters \(\theta\). In a Gaussian mixture these are weights \(\pi_k\), means \(\mu_k\), and covariances \(\Sigma_k\). The unobserved labels \(Z\) are latent variables whose conditional distribution is computed in the E-step.

E-step: compute the posterior distribution of the latent variables using the observed data and the current parameters, then form the expected complete-data log-likelihood.

M-step: update the parameters by maximizing that expectation. For MAP, also include the log-prior.

SymbolMeaning
\(\displaystyle X\)Observed data, held fixed during estimation.
\(\displaystyle Z\)Unobserved latent variables, such as mixture-component labels.
\(\displaystyle \theta\)Unknown model parameters.
\(\displaystyle \theta^{(t)}\)Parameter estimate at iteration \(\displaystyle t\).
\(\displaystyle p(X,Z\mid\theta)\)Complete-data model: a joint probability mass function or density.
\(\displaystyle p(X\mid\theta)\)Observed-data model after marginalizing over the latent variables.

If both \(X\) and \(Z\) were observed, the complete-data likelihood would be:

\[L(\theta;X,Z)=p(X,Z\mid\theta)\]
Full derivation: Derivation From Complete Data To Observed Data ↓
  1. Initialize the parameters at random or at chosen starting values.
  2. Compute the latent posterior given the observed data and the current parameters.
  3. Update the parameters using the expected complete-data log-likelihood, or equivalently the expected sufficient statistics when available.
  4. Repeat the E- and M-steps until a convergence criterion is met.

For maximum-likelihood EM, exact E- and M-steps do not decrease the observed-data log-likelihood. For MAP-EM, they do not decrease the posterior objective \(\log p(X\mid\theta)+\log p(\theta)\); the likelihood alone may decrease. A global optimum is not guaranteed.

Full derivation: Derive The Lower Bound ↓

Entropy and KL Decomposition

Understand The Gap Between The Bound And The Likelihood

The ELBO separates into an expected complete-data log-likelihood and an entropy term.

Full derivation: Complete mathematical derivation ↓
\[\log p(X\mid\theta)=\mathcal L(q,\theta)+\operatorname{KL}\!\left(q(Z)\,\|\,p(Z\mid X,\theta)\right)\]
Full derivation: Derivation Expected Complete-Data Log-Likelihood Plus Entropy ↓

KL divergence is nonnegative. It is zero exactly when the two distributions agree, up to sets of probability zero. Thus the ELBO is tight when:

\[q(Z)=p(Z\mid X,\theta)\]

Matching \(q\) to the latent posterior makes the gap zero: \(\mathcal L(q,\theta)=\log p(X\mid\theta)\). This is the basis of the E-step.

E-Step and M-Step

Alternate Between The Latent Posterior And The Parameters

EM alternates between optimizing the latent distribution \(q\) and the parameters \(\theta\), holding the other fixed. This is coordinate ascent on the ELBO.

Full derivation: Derivation E-Step: Make The Bound Tight ↓
Full derivation: Derivation M-Step: Maximize The Expected Complete-Data Log-Likelihood ↓

Each exact EM iteration improves or preserves the observed-data log-likelihood. Under suitable regularity conditions, limit points are stationary points; monotonicity alone does not ensure a finite parameter limit or a global maximum. Initialization can affect the result.

Full derivation: Complete mathematical derivation ↓

EM For MAP Estimation

For MAP estimation, the objective also includes the log-prior on the parameters:

\[J(\theta)=\log p(X\mid\theta)+\log p(\theta)\]

The E-step is unchanged because \(\theta^{(t)}\) is held fixed while computing the posterior of \(Z\). The M-step becomes:

\[\theta^{(t+1)}=\underset{\theta}{\operatorname{arg\,max}}\;\left[Q(\theta\mid\theta^{(t)})+\log p(\theta)\right]\]

Equivalently, maximize \(\mathcal L(q,\theta)+\log p(\theta)\). Exact MAP-EM steps do not decrease \(J(\theta)\); the observed likelihood alone need not increase because the prior is also part of the objective.

Gaussian Mixture Model

Unknown Group Labels And Soft Assignments

Imagine clustering people’s heights into two groups without knowing the group labels. If the labels were observed, each group’s Gaussian mean and variance could be fitted separately. EM instead uses probabilities of group membership.

  1. Start with a rough guess for the Gaussian parameters and mixing weights.
  2. For each observation, compute the probability that it belongs to each Gaussian.
  3. Use these soft assignments to recompute the parameters.
  4. Repeat.

For the general model, let \(X=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) contain independent observations with \(x_i\in\mathbb R^d\), generated from a mixture of \(K\) Gaussian components. Introduce a latent component label for each observation:

\[z_i\in\{1,\ldots,K\}\]
StepModel
Choose A Component
\[P(z_i=k\mid\theta)=\pi_k\]
\[\sum_{k=1}^{K}\pi_k=1,\qquad\pi_k\geq 0\]
Generate An Observation
\[x_i\mid z_i=k\sim\mathcal N(\mu_k,\Sigma_k)\]
Collect The Parameters
\[\theta=\{\pi_k,\mu_k,\Sigma_k\}_{k=1}^{K}\]

Here \(\mu_k\) is a component mean vector and \(\Sigma_k\) is its covariance matrix. For a nonsingular Gaussian density, the covariance is positive definite.

The logarithm of the mixture sum couples the component parameters, so a direct maximization generally has no simple closed-form solution. EM turns this into repeated weighted fits.

Full derivation: Derivation Marginalize The Component Labels ↓

Gaussian Mixture E- and M-Steps

E-Step: Compute Soft Memberships

At iteration \(t\), compute the responsibility of component \(k\) for observation \(x_i\). It is the posterior probability that the observation came from that component.

Each point has soft membership across the components. These probabilities are computed using the current parameters and are then held fixed throughout the M-step.

Earlier derivations: Why the EM lower bound is valid

Full derivation: Derivation E-Step: Responsibilities From Bayes’ Rule ↓
Full derivation: Derivation From Hidden Indicators To A Weighted Objective ↓

M-Step: Refit Each Component

Define the effective number of observations assigned to component \(k\):

\[N_k=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\gamma_{ik},\qquad\sum_{k=1}^{K}N_k=n\]

For \(N_k>0\), the M-step updates are:

ParameterUpdate
Mixing Weight
\[\pi_k^{(t+1)}=\frac{N_k}{n}\]
Mean
\[\mu_k^{(t+1)}=\frac{1}{N_k}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\gamma_{ik}x_i\]
Covariance
\[\Sigma_k^{(t+1)}=\frac{1}{N_k}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\gamma_{ik}(x_i-\mu_k^{(t+1)})(x_i-\mu_k^{(t+1)})^{\mathsf T}\]

All three updates use the same E-step responsibilities. The covariance is centered on the newly updated mean. In one dimension, the outer product becomes a squared deviation and the covariance becomes a variance.

Full derivation: Derivation Derive The Mixing-Weight Update ↓
Full derivation: Derivation Derive The Weighted-Mean Update ↓

The M-step fits each Gaussian using fractional membership weights. \(N_k\) replaces the group’s ordinary count, and the resulting weighted mean and covariance replace the corresponding fully observed estimates.

Full derivation: Derivation Derive The Weighted-Covariance Update ↓

Two-Gaussian Example

Example

One Complete EM Iteration

Model
I.i.d. observations from a mixture of two univariate normal distributions, with unobserved component labels. The number of components is fixed at \(K=2\).
Parameters to estimate
The weights \(\pi_1,\pi_2\) with \(\pi_1+\pi_2=1\), means \(\mu_1,\mu_2\), and variances \(\sigma_1^2,\sigma_2^2\). The initial values are starting guesses; equal initial variances do not constrain the fitted variances to remain equal.

Fit a two-component Gaussian mixture to the six observations:

\[x=[1.0,\;1.3,\;2.2,\;8.0,\;8.4,\;9.1]\]

Initialize all the parameters:

\[\pi_1^{(0)}=\pi_2^{(0)}=0.5,\qquad\mu_1^{(0)}=2,\qquad\mu_2^{(0)}=8\]
\[(\sigma_1^2)^{(0)}=(\sigma_2^2)^{(0)}=1\]

E-Step

The equal mixing weights and equal initial variances simplify the responsibility calculation. The common Gaussian normalizing factors cancel:

\(\displaystyle x_i\)\(\displaystyle \gamma_{i1}\)\(\displaystyle \gamma_{i2}\)
\(\displaystyle 1.0\)\(\displaystyle 0.999999999962\)\(\displaystyle 3.7751\times 10^{-11}\)
\(\displaystyle 1.3\)\(\displaystyle 0.999999999772\)\(\displaystyle 2.2838\times 10^{-10}\)
\(\displaystyle 2.2\)\(\displaystyle 0.999999949435\)\(\displaystyle 5.0565\times 10^{-8}\)
\(\displaystyle 8.0\)\(\displaystyle 1.5230\times 10^{-8}\)\(\displaystyle 0.999999984770\)
\(\displaystyle 8.4\)\(\displaystyle 1.3816\times 10^{-9}\)\(\displaystyle 0.999999998618\)
\(\displaystyle 9.1\)\(\displaystyle 2.0718\times 10^{-11}\)\(\displaystyle 0.999999999979\)
Derivation Calculate Responsibilities From The Initial Parameters
\(\displaystyle \gamma_{i1}\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{\exp\!\left[-\frac{(x_i-2)^2}{2}\right]}{\exp\!\left[-\frac{(x_i-2)^2}{2}\right]+\exp\!\left[-\frac{(x_i-8)^2}{2}\right]}\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{1}{1+\exp\!\left[\frac{(x_i-2)^2-(x_i-8)^2}{2}\right]}\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{1}{1+\exp(6x_i-30)}\)
\[\gamma_{i2}=1-\gamma_{i1}\]

For example, at \(x_i=2.2\):

\(\displaystyle \gamma_{i1}\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{1}{1+\exp(6\cdot2.2-30)}\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{1}{1+\exp(-16.8)}\)\(\approx\)\(\displaystyle 0.999999949435\)
\[\gamma_{i2}\approx5.0565\times10^{-8}\]

Values are rounded for display. The first three observations have responsibilities very close to one for component 1, while the last three have responsibilities very close to one for component 2. The assignments are still probabilities, rather than exact zero-or-one labels.

M-Step

Keep these responsibilities fixed. Their sums give:

Derivation Update Mixing Weights, Means And Variances
\[\pi_1^{(1)}=\frac{N_1}{6}\approx0.5,\qquad\pi_2^{(1)}=\frac{N_2}{6}\approx0.5\]

The weighted means are almost the ordinary means of the two separated groups:

\(\displaystyle \mu_1^{(1)}\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{\gamma_{11}(1.0)+\gamma_{21}(1.3)+\gamma_{31}(2.2)+\gamma_{41}(8.0)+\gamma_{51}(8.4)+\gamma_{61}(9.1)}{N_1}\)\(\approx\)\(\displaystyle \frac{1.0+1.3+2.2}{3}\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle 1.5\)
\(\displaystyle \mu_2^{(1)}\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{\gamma_{12}(1.0)+\gamma_{22}(1.3)+\gamma_{32}(2.2)+\gamma_{42}(8.0)+\gamma_{52}(8.4)+\gamma_{62}(9.1)}{N_2}\)\(\approx\)\(\displaystyle \frac{8.0+8.4+9.1}{3}\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle 8.5\)

Update the variances around those new means, using the same responsibility weights:

\(\displaystyle (\sigma_1^2)^{(1)}\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i=1}^{6}\gamma_{i1}(x_i-\mu_1^{(1)})^2\)\(\approx\)\(\displaystyle \frac{(1.0-1.5)^2+(1.3-1.5)^2+(2.2-1.5)^2}{3}\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{0.25+0.04+0.49}{3}=0.26\)
\(\displaystyle (\sigma_2^2)^{(1)}\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{1}{N_2}\sum_{i=1}^{6}\gamma_{i2}(x_i-\mu_2^{(1)})^2\)\(\approx\)\(\displaystyle \frac{(8.0-8.5)^2+(8.4-8.5)^2+(9.1-8.5)^2}{3}\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{0.25+0.01+0.36}{3}\approx0.206667\)
\[N_1\approx2.999999965801,\qquad N_2\approx3.000000034199\]

Using the unrounded responsibilities gives the following parameter values after one full iteration:

ParameterComponent 1Component 2
Mixing Weight\(\displaystyle 0.49999999\)\(\displaystyle 0.50000001\)
Mean\(\displaystyle 1.50000002\)\(\displaystyle 8.49999990\)
Variance\(\displaystyle 0.26000023\)\(\displaystyle 0.20666734\)
\[\ell(\theta^{(0)})\approx-11.122514,\qquad\ell(\theta^{(1)})\approx-8.286932\]

The observed-data log-likelihood increases. Recompute responsibilities with the updated parameters and repeat the E- and M-steps until the likelihood improvement and parameter changes are sufficiently small.

Limitations and Practical Choices

Initialization, Convergence And Degeneracy

  • Local solutions: EM can converge to a local optimum or another stationary point; a global optimum is not guaranteed.
  • Initialization: different starting values can produce different fitted parameters and likelihood values.
  • Slow convergence: likelihood improvements can become very small near a stationary point.
  • Mixture degeneracy: an unconstrained Gaussian component can collapse around an observation as its covariance approaches a singular matrix. The likelihood can become unbounded, so a finite unconstrained MLE may not exist.

For Gaussian mixtures in practice:

  • Run EM from several initializations and compare the final objective values.
  • Use k-means to initialize component locations and memberships.
  • Constrain or regularize covariance matrices to prevent collapse.
  • Monitor the observed-data log-likelihood throughout fitting, or the posterior objective for MAP-EM.

A component with \(N_k=0\) has no effective observations and its mean and covariance updates are undefined; it needs to be reinitialized or otherwise handled by the fitting procedure.

The monotonicity guarantee applies to the objective actually optimized. A prior or explicit covariance constraint changes that objective or its feasible parameter set and should be included consistently in the fitting steps.

Derivations and full mathematical details

All original proofs and intermediate calculations are retained below. The links in the sections above lead here.

From: Latent Variables And The EM Idea ↑
Derivation From Complete Data To Observed Data

Because only \(X\) is observed, the likelihood used for MLE sums or integrates over all possible latent values. For continuous \(Z\):

\(\displaystyle L(\theta;X)\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle p(X\mid\theta)\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \int p(X,Z\mid\theta)\,dZ\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \int p(X\mid Z,\theta)p(Z\mid\theta)\,dZ\)

For discrete latent variables, replace the integral by a sum. The model specifies the distribution of \(Z\) for each parameter value; the difficulty is that marginalization and the resulting optimization can be complicated.

From: Current topic ↑

Derive the Lower Bound

From Marginal Likelihood To The ELBO

The MLE objective is the observed-data log-likelihood. For discrete latent variables:

\[\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}=\underset{\theta}{\operatorname{arg\,max}}\;\ell(\theta)\]
Derivation The Logarithm Of A Sum
\(\displaystyle p(X\mid\theta)\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \sum_Z p(X,Z\mid\theta)\)
\(\displaystyle \ell(\theta)\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \log p(X\mid\theta)\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \log\sum_Z p(X,Z\mid\theta)\)

The sum is inside the logarithm, so the latent contributions cannot simply be separated into a sum of log-likelihoods. EM instead constructs and maximizes a lower bound.

Define the evidence lower bound (ELBO):

\[\mathcal L(q,\theta)=\sum_Z q(Z)\log p(X,Z\mid\theta)-\sum_Z q(Z)\log q(Z)\]

Introduce An Expectation And Apply Jensen’s Inequality

Introduce an auxiliary probability distribution \(q(Z)\) over the latent variables:

\[q(Z)\geq 0,\qquad\sum_Z q(Z)=1\]

For the following rewriting, take \(q(Z)>0\) wherever \(p(X,Z\mid\theta)>0\), so no contributing latent value is omitted. Multiply and divide each joint-probability term by \(q(Z)\):

\(\displaystyle p(X\mid\theta)\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \sum_Z p(X,Z\mid\theta)\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \sum_Z q(Z)\frac{p(X,Z\mid\theta)}{q(Z)}\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \mathbb E_q\!\left[\frac{p(X,Z\mid\theta)}{q(Z)}\right]\)

Taking a logarithm gives:

\(\displaystyle \log p(X\mid\theta)\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \log\sum_Z q(Z)\frac{p(X,Z\mid\theta)}{q(Z)}\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \log\mathbb E_q\!\left[\frac{p(X,Z\mid\theta)}{q(Z)}\right]\)

The logarithm is concave. Therefore, Jensen’s inequality for a positive random variable \(Y\) gives:

\[\log\mathbb E_q[Y]\geq\mathbb E_q[\log Y]\]

Apply this to \(Y=\frac{p(X,Z\mid\theta)}{q(Z)}\):

\(\displaystyle \log p(X\mid\theta)\)
\(\geq\)\(\displaystyle \mathbb E_q\!\left[\log\frac{p(X,Z\mid\theta)}{q(Z)}\right]\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \sum_Z q(Z)\log\frac{p(X,Z\mid\theta)}{q(Z)}\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \sum_Z q(Z)\log p(X,Z\mid\theta)-\sum_Z q(Z)\log q(Z)\)
\[\mathcal L(q,\theta)\leq\log p(X\mid\theta)\]

The same derivation applies to continuous latent variables with integrals in place of sums and suitable support and integrability conditions.

From: Entropy And KL Decomposition ↑

Derive The KL Decomposition From Bayes’ Rule

Bayes’ rule relates the joint model to the posterior distribution of the latent variables:

\[p(Z\mid X,\theta)=\frac{p(X,Z\mid\theta)}{p(X\mid\theta)}\]
\[p(X,Z\mid\theta)=p(Z\mid X,\theta)p(X\mid\theta)\]
\[\log p(X,Z\mid\theta)=\log p(Z\mid X,\theta)+\log p(X\mid\theta)\]

Take an expectation under \(q\). Since \(\log p(X\mid\theta)\) does not depend on \(Z\), it comes out of the expectation:

\(\displaystyle \mathbb E_q[\log p(X,Z\mid\theta)]\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \mathbb E_q[\log p(Z\mid X,\theta)]+\mathbb E_q[\log p(X\mid\theta)]\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \mathbb E_q[\log p(Z\mid X,\theta)]+\log p(X\mid\theta)\)

Substitute into the lower-bound formula:

\(\displaystyle \mathcal L(q,\theta)\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \mathbb E_q[\log p(X,Z\mid\theta)]-\mathbb E_q[\log q(Z)]\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \log p(X\mid\theta)+\mathbb E_q[\log p(Z\mid X,\theta)]-\mathbb E_q[\log q(Z)]\)

Rearranging isolates the difference between the observed log-likelihood and the bound:

\[\log p(X\mid\theta)=\mathcal L(q,\theta)+\mathbb E_q[\log q(Z)]-\mathbb E_q[\log p(Z\mid X,\theta)]\]
\(\displaystyle \mathbb E_q[\log q(Z)]-\mathbb E_q[\log p(Z\mid X,\theta)]\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \sum_Z q(Z)\left[\log q(Z)-\log p(Z\mid X,\theta)\right]\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \sum_Z q(Z)\log\frac{q(Z)}{p(Z\mid X,\theta)}\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \operatorname{KL}\!\left(q(Z)\,\|\,p(Z\mid X,\theta)\right)\)
From: Entropy And KL Decomposition ↑
Derivation Expected Complete-Data Log-Likelihood Plus Entropy
\(\displaystyle \mathcal L(q,\theta)\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \sum_Z q(Z)\log p(X,Z\mid\theta)-\sum_Z q(Z)\log q(Z)\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \mathbb E_q[\log p(X,Z\mid\theta)]-\mathbb E_q[\log q(Z)]\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \mathbb E_q[\log p(X,Z\mid\theta)]+H(q)\)
\[H(q)=-\mathbb E_q[\log q(Z)]=-\sum_Z q(Z)\log q(Z)\]

The first term averages the complete-data log-likelihood under \(q\). The second term is the entropy of \(q\) and depends on the latent distribution, not directly on \(\theta\). For continuous latent variables, the corresponding integral defines differential entropy.

From: E-Step And M-Step ↑
Derivation E-Step: Make The Bound Tight

Fix \(\theta=\theta^{(t)}\) and choose \(q\) to maximize \(\mathcal L(q,\theta^{(t)})\):

\[\log p(X\mid\theta^{(t)})=\mathcal L(q,\theta^{(t)})+\operatorname{KL}\!\left(q\,\|\,p(Z\mid X,\theta^{(t)})\right)\]

Earlier derivations: Jensen lower bound used by EM

The left side is constant with respect to \(q\). Maximizing the ELBO therefore minimizes the KL divergence. Its minimum is zero, attained at the current latent posterior:

\(\displaystyle q^{(t+1)}(Z)\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle p(Z\mid X,\theta^{(t)})\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{p(X,Z\mid\theta^{(t)})}{p(X\mid\theta^{(t)})}\)

Use this distribution to average the complete-data log-likelihood. The expectation is taken over \(Z\); the candidate parameters \(\theta\) inside the logarithm remain free:

\(\displaystyle Q(\theta\mid\theta^{(t)})\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \mathbb E_{Z\sim p(Z\mid X,\theta^{(t)})}[\log p(X,Z\mid\theta)]\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \sum_Z q^{(t+1)}(Z)\log p(X,Z\mid\theta)\)
From: E-Step And M-Step ↑
Derivation M-Step: Maximize The Expected Complete-Data Log-Likelihood

Now hold \(q=q^{(t+1)}\) fixed and maximize the bound with respect to \(\theta\):

\(\displaystyle \mathcal L(q^{(t+1)},\theta)\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \mathbb E_{q^{(t+1)}}[\log p(X,Z\mid\theta)]-\mathbb E_{q^{(t+1)}}[\log q^{(t+1)}(Z)]\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle Q(\theta\mid\theta^{(t)})+H(q^{(t+1)})\)

The entropy term is fixed during this step. Consequently:

\(\displaystyle \theta^{(t+1)}\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \underset{\theta}{\operatorname{arg\,max}}\;\mathcal L(q^{(t+1)},\theta)\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \underset{\theta}{\operatorname{arg\,max}}\;Q(\theta\mid\theta^{(t)})\)
From: E-Step And M-Step ↑

Why The Log-Likelihood Cannot Decrease

The E-step makes the bound equal to the old log-likelihood. The M-step increases or preserves that bound, and the new log-likelihood is at least as large as the new bound:

\(\displaystyle \ell(\theta^{(t)})\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \mathcal L(q^{(t+1)},\theta^{(t)})\)\(\leq\)\(\displaystyle \mathcal L(q^{(t+1)},\theta^{(t+1)})\)\(\leq\)\(\displaystyle \ell(\theta^{(t+1)})\)

The first equality follows from the tight E-step bound; the first inequality follows from the M-step maximization; the second inequality is the ELBO property.

From: Gaussian Mixture Model ↑
Derivation Marginalize The Component Labels
\(\displaystyle p(x_i\mid\theta)\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \sum_{k=1}^{K}p(x_i,z_i=k\mid\theta)\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \sum_{k=1}^{K}p(x_i\mid z_i=k,\theta)P(z_i=k\mid\theta)\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \sum_{k=1}^{K}\pi_k\mathcal N(x_i\mid\mu_k,\Sigma_k)\)

Independence across observations gives:

\[L(\theta;X)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\pi_k\mathcal N(x_i\mid\mu_k,\Sigma_k)\]
\(\displaystyle \ell(\theta)\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^{n}\log p(x_i\mid\theta)\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^{K}\pi_k\mathcal N(x_i\mid\mu_k,\Sigma_k)\right)\)
From: Gaussian Mixture E- And M-Steps ↑
Derivation E-Step: Responsibilities From Bayes’ Rule
\(\displaystyle \gamma_{ik}\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle P(z_i=k\mid x_i,\theta^{(t)})\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{p(x_i\mid z_i=k,\theta^{(t)})P(z_i=k\mid\theta^{(t)})}{p(x_i\mid\theta^{(t)})}\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{\pi_k^{(t)}\mathcal N(x_i\mid\mu_k^{(t)},\Sigma_k^{(t)})}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\pi_j^{(t)}\mathcal N(x_i\mid\mu_j^{(t)},\Sigma_j^{(t)})}\)

The denominator sums the weighted densities across all components and normalizes the responsibilities for each observation:

\[0\leq\gamma_{ik}\leq 1,\qquad\sum_{k=1}^{K}\gamma_{ik}=1\]
From: Gaussian Mixture E- And M-Steps ↑
Derivation From Hidden Indicators To A Weighted Objective

To connect the general EM objective to the Gaussian updates, let \(I_{ik}=\mathbf 1\{z_i=k\}\) indicate which component generated observation \(i\). With the labels observed:

\[p(X,Z\mid\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\prod_{k=1}^{K}\left[\pi_k\mathcal N(x_i\mid\mu_k,\Sigma_k)\right]^{I_{ik}}\]
\(\displaystyle \log p(X,Z\mid\theta)\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{k=1}^{K}I_{ik}\log\!\left[\pi_k\mathcal N(x_i\mid\mu_k,\Sigma_k)\right]\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{k=1}^{K}I_{ik}\left[\log\pi_k+\log\mathcal N(x_i\mid\mu_k,\Sigma_k)\right]\)

The posterior expectation of an indicator is its posterior probability:

\[\mathbb E[I_{ik}\mid X,\theta^{(t)}]=\gamma_{ik}\]

Taking the expectation therefore replaces the unknown indicators by responsibilities:

\[Q(\theta\mid\theta^{(t)})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\gamma_{ik}\left[\log\pi_k+\log\mathcal N(x_i\mid\mu_k,\Sigma_k)\right]\]
From: Gaussian Mixture E- And M-Steps ↑
Derivation Derive The Mixing-Weight Update

The part of \(Q\) that involves the mixing weights is \(\sum_k N_k\log\pi_k\). Enforce \(\sum_k\pi_k=1\) with a Lagrange multiplier:

\[\mathcal A=\sum_{k=1}^{K}N_k\log\pi_k+\lambda\left(1-\sum_{k=1}^{K}\pi_k\right)\]
\[\frac{\partial\mathcal A}{\partial\pi_k}=\frac{N_k}{\pi_k}-\lambda=0\]
\[\pi_k=\frac{N_k}{\lambda}\]
\(\displaystyle 1\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \sum_{k=1}^{K}\pi_k\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{1}{\lambda}\sum_{k=1}^{K}N_k\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{n}{\lambda}\)
\[\lambda=n\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\pi_k^{(t+1)}=\frac{N_k}{n}\]
From: Gaussian Mixture E- And M-Steps ↑
Derivation Derive The Weighted-Mean Update

For a \(d\)-dimensional Gaussian, the log-density is:

\[\log\mathcal N(x_i\mid\mu_k,\Sigma_k)=-\frac{d}{2}\log(2\pi)-\frac{1}{2}\log|\Sigma_k|-\frac{1}{2}(x_i-\mu_k)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_k^{-1}(x_i-\mu_k)\]

Only the quadratic term depends on \(\mu_k\). Differentiate the weighted objective, treating the responsibilities and covariance as fixed:

\(\displaystyle \frac{\partial Q}{\partial\mu_k}\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^{n}\gamma_{ik}\Sigma_k^{-1}(x_i-\mu_k)\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \Sigma_k^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\gamma_{ik}x_i-N_k\mu_k\right)\)

Set the gradient to zero and multiply by the invertible covariance matrix:

\[\sum_{i=1}^{n}\gamma_{ik}x_i-N_k\mu_k=0\]
\[N_k\mu_k=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\gamma_{ik}x_i\]
\[\mu_k^{(t+1)}=\frac{1}{N_k}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\gamma_{ik}x_i\]
From: Gaussian Mixture E- And M-Steps ↑
Derivation Derive The Weighted-Covariance Update

With the mean updated, define the weighted scatter matrix:

\[S_k=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\gamma_{ik}(x_i-\mu_k^{(t+1)})(x_i-\mu_k^{(t+1)})^{\mathsf T}\]

Use the trace identity \(v^{\mathsf T}Av=\operatorname{tr}(Avv^{\mathsf T})\) to collect the weighted quadratic terms:

\[\sum_{i=1}^{n}\gamma_{ik}(x_i-\mu_k^{(t+1)})^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_k^{-1}(x_i-\mu_k^{(t+1)})=\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_k^{-1}S_k)\]

Writing \(C\) for terms independent of the covariance, the component objective is:

\[Q_k=C-\frac{N_k}{2}\log|\Sigma_k|-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_k^{-1}S_k)\]

Let \(\Lambda_k=\Sigma_k^{-1}\) be the precision matrix. Since \(\log|\Sigma_k|=-\log|\Lambda_k|\), this becomes:

\[Q_k=C+\frac{N_k}{2}\log|\Lambda_k|-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tr}(\Lambda_k S_k)\]

Using \(\frac{\partial\log|\Lambda_k|}{\partial\Lambda_k}=\Lambda_k^{-\mathsf T}\) and \(\frac{\partial\operatorname{tr}(\Lambda_k S_k)}{\partial\Lambda_k}=S_k^{\mathsf T}\), and the symmetry of both matrices:

\[\frac{\partial Q_k}{\partial\Lambda_k}=\frac{N_k}{2}\Lambda_k^{-1}-\frac{1}{2}S_k=0\]
\[N_k\Lambda_k^{-1}=S_k\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\Sigma_k^{(t+1)}=\frac{S_k}{N_k}\]
\[\Sigma_k^{(t+1)}=\frac{1}{N_k}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\gamma_{ik}(x_i-\mu_k^{(t+1)})(x_i-\mu_k^{(t+1)})^{\mathsf T}\]

When \(S_k\) is positive definite, this is the interior maximum of the covariance objective. Singular scatter matrices lead to the degeneracy discussed below.

Fisher Information / Cramér–Rao

Connect the score and Fisher information to bounds on the variance of unbiased estimators.

The Bound, Score and Information

A Lower Bound On Estimator Variance

The Cramér–Rao bound gives a lower bound on the variance of an unbiased estimator. Under the regularity conditions below, the bound is the reciprocal of the Fisher information in the observed data:

Model
A probability mass function or density \(p(x;\theta)\) satisfying the stated regularity conditions. The examples use independent Bernoulli flips and normal observations.
Parameters to estimate
The parameter \(\theta\): specifically the head probability \(p\) or the normal mean \(\mu\) with known variance. We derive a lower bound on the variance of an estimator of the chosen parameter.
\[\operatorname{Var}_\theta(\hat\theta)\geq\frac{1}{I(\theta)}\]

Here \(X\) denotes the observed data, which may be a single observation or an entire sample, and \(p(x;\theta)\) denotes its probability density or mass function. The estimator \(\hat\theta(X)\) is a function of those data; its definition does not depend on the unknown parameter.

QuantityDefinition
Unbiased Estimator
\[\mathbb E_\theta[\hat\theta(X)]=\theta\]
Log-Likelihood
\[\ell(\theta;X)=\log p(X;\theta)\]
Score
\[U(X;\theta)=\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log p(X;\theta)\]
Fisher Information
\[I(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta[U(X;\theta)^2]\]

The score measures the local sensitivity of the log-likelihood to the parameter. Fisher information averages the squared score over repeated data drawn from the model at \(\theta\). The information is a property of the model and the observation scheme, rather than of the estimator.

More Fisher information gives a smaller variance lower bound. The bound need not be attainable in every model. An unbiased estimator that attains it is called efficient.

Regularity Conditions

The scalar derivation uses the following regular setting:

  • The parameter lies in the interior of its parameter space, and the model has a common support that does not depend on the parameter.
  • The density or mass function is differentiable in the parameter, and differentiation may be interchanged with the integrals or sums used below.
  • The estimator has finite variance and is unbiased throughout a neighborhood of the parameter value.
  • The information satisfies \(0<I(\theta)<\infty\).

The second-derivative form of Fisher information also requires sufficient twice-differentiability and a valid interchange of second derivatives with integration or summation. If these conditions fail, the usual formulas and bound require separate justification.

The proof is written with integrals for continuous data. For discrete data with fixed support, the same steps use sums.

Full derivation: Derive The Scalar Bound ↓

Fisher Information Identities

The Expected-Curvature Form

Under the stated regularity conditions, Fisher information has two equivalent forms:

FormExpression
Expected Squared Score
\[I(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log p(X;\theta)\right)^2\right]\]
Expected Negative Curvature
\[I(\theta)=-\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}\log p(X;\theta)\right]\]

Fisher information is the expected negative curvature of the log-likelihood. A larger value indicates greater average local sensitivity to changes in the parameter.

Full derivation: Complete mathematical derivation ↓

Information In Independent Samples

For \(n\) independent observations with respective densities or mass functions \(p_i(x_i;\theta)\), the joint likelihood factors into a product. Taking a logarithm gives a sum:

\[p(x_1,\ldots,x_n;\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}p_i(x_i;\theta)\]
\[\ell_n(\theta)=\log p(X_1,\ldots,X_n;\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log p_i(X_i;\theta)\]
Full derivation: Complete mathematical derivation ↓
\[\operatorname{Var}_\theta(\hat\theta)\geq\frac{1}{I_n(\theta)}=\frac{1}{nI_1(\theta)}\]

For independent observations, information is the sum of the individual information values. For i.i.d. observations, it is \(n\) times the information in one observation. The factor \(n\) is already included when using \(I_n\).

Bernoulli Coin-Flip Example

Example

Estimate The Probability Of Heads

Model
Independent Bernoulli flips with common probability \(p\) and \(0<p<1\).
Parameters to estimate
The head probability \(p\). Compute the Fisher information and variance lower bound for an unbiased estimator of \(p\).

A coin has an unknown probability of heads \(p\). Code a head as 1 and a tail as 0. For one flip:

\[X\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p),\qquad X\in\{0,1\},\qquad 0<p<1\]

The likelihood and log-likelihood for one observed flip are:

\[P(X=x\mid p)=p^x(1-p)^{1-x}\]
Derivation Compute The Score And Fisher Information

Differentiate with respect to the probability parameter:

\(\displaystyle U(x;p)\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{\partial\ell(p;x)}{\partial p}\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{x}{p}-\frac{1-x}{1-p}\)

Differentiate again:

\[\frac{\partial^2\ell(p;x)}{\partial p^2}=-\frac{x}{p^2}-\frac{1-x}{(1-p)^2}\]

Use \(\mathbb E_p[X]=p\) and \(\mathbb E_p[1-X]=1-p\) in the negative expected second derivative:

\(\displaystyle I_1(p)\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle -\mathbb E_p\!\left[\frac{\partial^2\ell(p;X)}{\partial p^2}\right]\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle -\left(-\frac{\mathbb E_p[X]}{p^2}-\frac{\mathbb E_p[1-X]}{(1-p)^2}\right)\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle -\left(-\frac{p}{p^2}-\frac{1-p}{(1-p)^2}\right)\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{1-p}\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{1-p+p}{p(1-p)}\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{1}{p(1-p)}\)
\[\ell(p;x)=x\log p+(1-x)\log(1-p)\]

For \(n\) independent flips of the same coin:

\[I_n(p)=nI_1(p)=\frac{n}{p(1-p)}\]

Thus every unbiased estimator of \(p\) based on these flips satisfies:

\[\operatorname{Var}_p(\hat p)\geq\frac{1}{I_n(p)}=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}\]

The sample proportion is unbiased. Its variance p(1 − p)/n equals 1/Iₙ(p), so it attains the bound. Sample-proportion moments

\[\hat p=\bar X=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i\]

The sample proportion is unbiased and its variance is exactly the Cramér–Rao lower bound. It is therefore an efficient estimator of the coin’s probability of heads.

Normal Mean Example

Example

Estimate The Mean Of A Normal Distribution

Model
I.i.d. normal observations, \(X_i\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), with known \(\sigma^2>0\).
Parameters to estimate
The population mean \(\mu\). Compute the information and variance lower bound while holding the variance fixed.

Let the observations be independent and identically distributed as:

\[X_1,\ldots,X_n\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\]

Estimate the mean \(\mu\), treating the population variance \(\sigma^2>0\) as known in this scalar calculation.

For one observation, the log-likelihood is:

Derivation Compute Information About The Normal Mean

Differentiate with respect to the mean:

\(\displaystyle U(x;\mu)\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{\partial}{\partial\mu}\log p(x;\mu)\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\,2(x-\mu)(-1)\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{x-\mu}{\sigma^2}\)

The mean of the score is zero since \(\mathbb E_\mu[X-\mu]=0\). The information in one observation is:

\(\displaystyle I_1(\mu)\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \mathbb E_\mu\!\left[\left(\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma^2}\right)^2\right]\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{1}{\sigma^4}\mathbb E_\mu[(X-\mu)^2]\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{1}{\sigma^4}\operatorname{Var}_\mu(X)\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^4}\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\)
\[\log p(x;\mu)=-\frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2)-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\]

The information from \(n\) i.i.d. observations and the corresponding variance bound are:

\[I_n(\mu)=\frac{n}{\sigma^2}\]
\[\operatorname{Var}_\mu(\hat\mu)\geq\frac{1}{I_n(\mu)}=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\]

The sample mean is unbiased and attains the normal-mean bound: Var(X̄) = σ²/n = 1/Iₙ(μ). Unbiasedness · Variance derivation

\[\bar X=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i,\qquad\mathbb E_\mu[\bar X]=\mu\]

The sample mean is an efficient unbiased estimator of the normal mean: its variance is exactly the Cramér–Rao lower bound.

Matrix Form

Several Unknown Parameters

When the parameter is a vector \(\boldsymbol\theta=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_d)^{\mathsf T}\), the score is a vector and Fisher information is a \(d\times d\) matrix. Here \(d\) counts parameters, while \(n\) counts observations.

\[\mathbf U(X;\boldsymbol\theta)=\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\log f(X;\boldsymbol\theta)\]

Earlier derivations: Scalar Cramér–Rao derivation

\[\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)=\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}\!\left[\mathbf U(X;\boldsymbol\theta)\mathbf U(X;\boldsymbol\theta)^{\mathsf T}\right]\]

The entry in row \(i\) and column \(j\) is:

\[[\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)]_{ij}=\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}\!\left[\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_i}\log f(X;\boldsymbol\theta)\right)\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_j}\log f(X;\boldsymbol\theta)\right)\right]\]

Under the corresponding second-derivative regularity conditions, the alternative form uses the expected negative Hessian:

\[\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)=-\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}\!\left[\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}^{2}\log f(X;\boldsymbol\theta)\right]\]
\[[\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)]_{ij}=-\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}\!\left[\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta_i\,\partial\theta_j}\log f(X;\boldsymbol\theta)\right]\]

If \(T(X)\) is an unbiased vector estimator of \(\boldsymbol\theta\) and the Fisher information matrix is positive definite, then:

\[\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[T(X)]=\boldsymbol\theta\]
\[\operatorname{Cov}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T(X))\succeq\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)^{-1}\]

The symbol \(\succeq\) means that the difference is positive semidefinite. For every vector \(a\):

\[a^{\mathsf T}\left[\operatorname{Cov}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T)-\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)^{-1}\right]a\geq0\]

For an individual parameter component \(\theta_m\), take the corresponding diagonal entry of the inverse matrix:

\[\operatorname{Var}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T_m)=[\operatorname{Cov}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T)]_{mm}\geq[\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)^{-1}]_{mm}\geq\frac{1}{[\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)]_{mm}}\]

Invert the full information matrix before taking the diagonal entry. In general, \([\mathcal I^{-1}]_{mm}\) differs from \(\frac{1}{\mathcal I_{mm}}\). They coincide when the score for that parameter has zero information cross-terms with the other unknown parameters, including when the information matrix is diagonal.

The reciprocal \(\frac{1}{\mathcal I_{mm}}\) is the scalar bound when the other parameters are treated as known; with other parameters unknown, the diagonal entry of the full inverse accounts for those nuisance parameters. The matrix here is the information in all the observed data. For i.i.d. observations, \(\mathcal I_n=n\mathcal I_1\).

Biased Estimators and Mean Squared Error

Extend The Bound To A Biased Estimator

An estimator need not be unbiased. Define its bias as:

\[b(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta[\hat\theta(X)]-\theta\]
Full derivation: Derivation Include The Derivative Of The Bias ↓
\[\operatorname{Var}_\theta(\hat\theta)\geq\frac{[1+b^{\prime}(\theta)]^2}{I(\theta)}\]

For a biased estimator, accuracy is also described by its mean squared error (MSE), which includes the squared bias.

Apply MSE = variance + squared bias, then substitute the variance lower bound to obtain the MSE bound below. Bias–variance decomposition · Biased-estimator variance bound

\[\operatorname{MSE}_\theta(\hat\theta)\geq\frac{[1+b^{\prime}(\theta)]^2}{I(\theta)}+b(\theta)^2\]

When \(b(\theta)\equiv0\), its derivative also vanishes and both bounds reduce to the usual unbiased Cramér–Rao bound. For an i.i.d. sample, use \(I_n(\theta)=nI_1(\theta)\) in the denominator.

Derivations and full mathematical details

All original proofs and intermediate calculations are retained below. The links in the sections above lead here.

From: Current topic ↑

Derive the Scalar Bound

From Unbiasedness To Cauchy–Schwarz

The key identity is that the covariance between an unbiased estimator and the score equals one. Cauchy–Schwarz then converts that identity into a variance bound.

The Score Has Mean Zero

Start with the logarithmic derivative:

\(\displaystyle U(x;\theta)\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log p(x;\theta)\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{1}{p(x;\theta)}\frac{\partial p(x;\theta)}{\partial\theta}\)

Equivalently, on the support of the density:

\[\frac{\partial p(x;\theta)}{\partial\theta}=p(x;\theta)U(x;\theta)\]

Taking the expectation of the score and differentiating the normalization of the density gives:

\(\displaystyle \mathbb E_\theta[U(X;\theta)]\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \int\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log p(x;\theta)\,p(x;\theta)\,dx\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \int\frac{1}{p(x;\theta)}\frac{\partial p(x;\theta)}{\partial\theta}\,p(x;\theta)\,dx\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \int\frac{\partial p(x;\theta)}{\partial\theta}\,dx\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\int p(x;\theta)\,dx\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}1=0\)

Differentiate The Unbiasedness Identity

For an unbiased estimator:

\(\displaystyle \mathbb E_\theta[\hat\theta(X)]\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \int\hat\theta(x)p(x;\theta)\,dx\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \theta\)

Differentiate both sides with respect to the parameter:

\[\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\int\hat\theta(x)p(x;\theta)\,dx=1\]

Interchange the derivative and integral. Since \(\hat\theta(x)\) depends only on the observed value \(x\), the derivative acts on the density:

\(\displaystyle 1\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \int\hat\theta(x)\frac{\partial p(x;\theta)}{\partial\theta}\,dx\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \int\hat\theta(x)p(x;\theta)\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log p(x;\theta)\,dx\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \int\hat\theta(x)U(x;\theta)p(x;\theta)\,dx\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \mathbb E_\theta[\hat\theta(X)U(X;\theta)]\)

Express The Identity As A Covariance

For any two random variables with finite second moments, write \(\mu_A=\mathbb E[A]\) and \(\mu_B=\mathbb E[B]\). Expanding the covariance gives:

\(\displaystyle \operatorname{Cov}(A,B)\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \mathbb E[(A-\mu_A)(B-\mu_B)]\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \mathbb E[AB]-\mu_A\mathbb E[B]-\mu_B\mathbb E[A]+\mu_A\mu_B\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \mathbb E[AB]-\mathbb E[A]\mathbb E[B]\)

In this case, \(\mathbb E_\theta[\hat\theta]=\theta\) and \(\mathbb E_\theta[U]=0\). Therefore the centering term vanishes:

\[\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[\mathbb E_\theta[\hat\theta]U\right]=\theta\mathbb E_\theta[U]=0\]
\(\displaystyle 1\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \mathbb E_\theta[\hat\theta U]\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \mathbb E_\theta[\hat\theta U]-\mathbb E_\theta[\hat\theta]\mathbb E_\theta[U]\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \mathbb E_\theta[(\hat\theta-\theta)U]\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \operatorname{Cov}_\theta(\hat\theta,U)\)

The score variance is its second moment because its mean is zero:

\(\displaystyle \operatorname{Var}_\theta(U)\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \mathbb E_\theta[U^2]-\left(\mathbb E_\theta[U]\right)^2\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \mathbb E_\theta[U^2]\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle I(\theta)\)
\[\boxed{\operatorname{Var}_\theta(\hat\theta)\geq\frac{1}{I(\theta)}}\]

This is the scalar Cramér–Rao lower bound for unbiased estimation of \(\theta\).

Apply Cauchy–Schwarz To Obtain The Bound

Apply Cauchy–Schwarz to the centered estimator and centered score:

\[\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(\hat\theta,U)^2\leq\operatorname{Var}_\theta(\hat\theta)\operatorname{Var}_\theta(U)\]

Substitute the covariance and score variance found above:

\[1^2\leq\operatorname{Var}_\theta(\hat\theta)I(\theta)\]

Divide by the positive information \(I(\theta)\):

\[\operatorname{Var}_\theta(\hat\theta)\geq\frac{1}{I(\theta)}\]
From: Fisher Information Identities ↑

Derive The Second-Derivative Form

Differentiate the logarithm a second time, keeping the data value fixed:

\(\displaystyle \frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}\log p(x;\theta)\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\left[\frac{1}{p(x;\theta)}\frac{\partial p(x;\theta)}{\partial\theta}\right]\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{1}{p(x;\theta)}\frac{\partial^2p(x;\theta)}{\partial\theta^2}-\frac{1}{p(x;\theta)^2}\left(\frac{\partial p(x;\theta)}{\partial\theta}\right)^2\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{1}{p(x;\theta)}\frac{\partial^2p(x;\theta)}{\partial\theta^2}-U(x;\theta)^2\)

Multiply by the density and integrate:

\(\displaystyle \mathbb E_\theta\!\left[\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}\log p(X;\theta)\right]\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \int\frac{\partial^2p(x;\theta)}{\partial\theta^2}\,dx-\mathbb E_\theta[U(X;\theta)^2]\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}\int p(x;\theta)\,dx-I(\theta)\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}1-I(\theta)\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle -I(\theta)\)
From: Fisher Information Identities ↑

Add The Information From Independent Observations

Differentiate the joint log-likelihood:

\(\displaystyle U_n(\theta)\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{\partial\ell_n(\theta)}{\partial\theta}\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log p_i(X_i;\theta)\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^{n}U_i(\theta)\)

Each individual score has mean zero. Independence of the observations makes the scores independent, so all cross-covariance terms vanish:

\(\displaystyle I_n(\theta)\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \operatorname{Var}_\theta\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}U_i\right)\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{Var}_\theta(U_i)+2\sum_{i<j}\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(U_i,U_j)\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^{n}I_i(\theta)\)

If the observations are also identically distributed, every individual information term equals \(I_1(\theta)\):

\[I_n(\theta)=nI_1(\theta)\]
From: Biased Estimators And Mean Squared Error ↑
Derivation Include The Derivative Of The Bias

Rewrite the expectation and differentiate:

\[\mathbb E_\theta[\hat\theta(X)]=\theta+b(\theta)\]
\(\displaystyle 1+b^{\prime}(\theta)\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\mathbb E_\theta[\hat\theta(X)]\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \int\hat\theta(x)\frac{\partial p(x;\theta)}{\partial\theta}\,dx\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \mathbb E_\theta[\hat\theta(X)U(X;\theta)]\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \operatorname{Cov}_\theta(\hat\theta,U)\)

The last equality again uses the zero mean of the score. Cauchy–Schwarz therefore gives:

\[[1+b^{\prime}(\theta)]^2\leq\operatorname{Var}_\theta(\hat\theta)I(\theta)\]
\[\operatorname{Var}_\theta(\hat\theta)\geq\frac{[1+b^{\prime}(\theta)]^2}{I(\theta)}\]

Uncertainty of Point Estimates

Additional concepts worth applying

Bootstrap validity depends on the statistic and sampling design

Resampling individual rows is reasonable only when those rows are the independent sampling units. For paired, clustered or time-indexed data, resample pairs, clusters or appropriate blocks.

Practical implication: Percentile, basic and bias-corrected accelerated (BCa) intervals can behave differently under skew. Naive bootstrap methods can fail for extreme-value or nonsmooth estimators such as the endpoint of a Uniform distribution.

Compare frequentist and Bayesian uncertainty calculations, including Wald, likelihood-ratio, and bootstrap methods.

Point Estimates and Uncertainty

From An Estimate To Uncertainty

After computing a point estimate, we need to quantify its uncertainty. In frequentist inference, this means characterizing the sampling variability of the estimator. Bayesian inference instead describes uncertainty about the parameter through its posterior distribution.

Model
A sampling model \(f(y\mid\theta)\) and, for Bayesian calculations, a specified prior. The examples use normal observations with known variance and independent Bernoulli coin flips.
Parameters to estimate
The normal mean \(\mu\) or head probability \(p\). After obtaining the point estimate, quantify either its repeated-sample variability or posterior uncertainty about the parameter.

A point estimate alone does not describe either kind of uncertainty. MLE and MAP each select one parameter value:

MethodPoint Estimate
Maximum Likelihood

Uses the data likelihood:

\[\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}=\underset{\theta}{\mathrm{arg\,max}}L(\theta)\]

Earlier derivations: Bias–variance identity

Maximum A Posteriori

Uses the likelihood plus a prior:

\(\displaystyle \hat\theta_{\mathrm{MAP}}\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \underset{\theta}{\mathrm{arg\,max}}p(\theta\mid y)\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \underset{\theta}{\mathrm{arg\,max}}\{\log L(\theta)+\log p(\theta)\}\)

Full Bayesian inference retains the posterior distribution of the parameter, rather than only its mode. That posterior is different from the repeated-sample distribution of an estimator.

ViewpointMeaning Of Uncertainty
Frequentist

If I repeated the experiment many times, how much would the estimator change?

The parameter is fixed and unknown. The estimate changes across repeated samples, so uncertainty is described by the estimator’s sampling distribution.

Bayesian

Given the observed data, what values of the parameter remain plausible?

Uncertainty is described by the posterior distribution of the parameter after seeing the data, conditional on the model and prior.

Confidence Intervals and Credible Intervals

Two Interpretations Of An Interval

A confidence interval and a credible interval express these different views of uncertainty. Write \(Y\) for random data before observation and \(y\) for the realized data.

IntervalProbability Statement And Interpretation
Confidence Interval
Frequentist

A 95% confidence interval procedure \(C(Y)\) with a finite-sample coverage guarantee satisfies:

\[P_{\theta_0}\!\left(\theta_0\in C(Y)\right)\geq0.95\quad\text{for every }\theta_0\]

This is a probability statement about the procedure. In repeated sampling, at least 95% of the intervals contain the fixed true parameter \(\theta_0\) in the long-run coverage sense. For a procedure with exactly 95% coverage, the probability equals 0.95.

Exact procedures for discrete data, such as Clopper–Pearson binomial intervals, can be conservative and have coverage above 95%. Once the data are observed, the realized interval either contains the parameter or does not. Approximate procedures aim for coverage close to the nominal level and need not satisfy this finite-sample guarantee.

Credible Interval
Bayesian

A 95% posterior credible interval \(C(y)\) satisfies:

\[P\!\left(\theta\in C(y)\mid y\right)=0.95\]

This is a probability statement about the parameter conditional on the observed data. Given the model and prior, there is 95% posterior probability that the parameter lies in this interval.

Bayesian uncertainty concerns the parameter given the observed data. Frequentist sampling uncertainty concerns how an estimator would vary across repeated datasets.

Frequentist Uncertainty with MLE and MAP

Sampling Variability Of The Estimator

In frequentist inference, the parameter is fixed and unknown, while the estimator is a random variable before the data are observed. Its uncertainty is therefore described by its sampling distribution.

For MLE, the classic tools are:

  1. Fisher information, asymptotic normality, and Wald intervals
  2. Likelihood-ratio intervals
  3. Bootstrap

MAP can also be studied from a frequentist viewpoint as a penalized estimator. The general idea of studying its repeated-sample behavior still applies, but the usual unpenalized MLE formulas do not automatically give the sampling uncertainty of a MAP estimator.

Fisher Information and the Wald Approximation

Information And Asymptotic Behavior

Fisher information describes the curvature of the likelihood and gives a large-sample normal approximation to the MLE’s sampling distribution. Consider independent, identically distributed observations, and let \(I_1(\theta)\) denote information in one observation.

Under regularity conditions, including a correctly specified, identifiable, sufficiently smooth model, an interior true parameter, and finite positive information:

\[\sqrt n\,\left(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}-\theta_0\right)\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N\!\left(0,I_1(\theta_0)^{-1}\right)\]

Earlier derivations: Score and information identities · Cramér–Rao bound

The scaled estimation error converges in distribution to a centered normal distribution. Equivalently, for a large sample:

\[\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}\ \sim\ \mathcal N\!\left(\theta_0,\frac{1}{n}I_1(\theta_0)^{-1}\right)\]

Keep information per observation separate from information in the full sample. With \(\ell_n(\theta)=\log L_n(\theta)\):

InformationDefinition
One Observation
\[I_1(\theta)=-\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}\log f(Y_1;\theta)\right]\]
Full Sample
\(\displaystyle I_n(\theta)\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle -\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[\frac{\partial^2\ell_n(\theta)}{\partial\theta^2}\right]\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle nI_1(\theta)\)

The sampling variance is therefore approximately \(I_n(\theta_0)^{-1}\). Since the true parameter is unknown, we can plug the MLE into the expected information or use the observed information, which is computed directly from the fitted log-likelihood:

\[J_n(\hat\theta)=-\left.\frac{\partial^2\ell_n(\theta)}{\partial\theta^2}\right|_{\theta=\hat\theta}\]

Unlike expected information, observed information does not average the curvature over possible datasets. Using the full-sample observed information gives:

\[\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\theta)\approx J_n(\hat\theta)^{-1}\]
\[\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\theta)\approx\sqrt{J_n(\hat\theta)^{-1}}\]

For a vector parameter, invert the full information matrix to estimate the covariance matrix. The standard error of each component is the square root of the corresponding diagonal element of that inverse.

The practical sequence is:

  1. Maximize the log-likelihood
  2. Compute its Hessian at the maximum
  3. Negate the Hessian to obtain observed information, then invert it
  4. Report standard errors and confidence intervals using the Wald approximation

Wald Confidence Intervals

The Wald approximation turns asymptotic normality into a hypothesis test or confidence interval. A scalar 95% Wald confidence interval is:

\(\displaystyle C_{\mathrm{Wald}}(y)\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \left[\hat\theta-z_{0.975}\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\theta),\ \hat\theta+z_{0.975}\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\theta)\right]\)\(\approx\)\(\displaystyle \left[\hat\theta-1.96\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\theta),\ \hat\theta+1.96\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\theta)\right]\)

This approximation is often useful for large samples when the log-likelihood is nearly quadratic. It can be poor with small samples, strong asymmetry, or estimates close to a parameter boundary.

Likelihood-Ratio Intervals

Use The Likelihood Shape

A likelihood-ratio interval uses the shape of the likelihood itself. For a scalar parameter, define the likelihood-ratio statistic:

\[R(\theta)=2\left[\ell_n(\hat\theta)-\ell_n(\theta)\right]\]

Under the regularity conditions for Wilks’ theorem, the statistic evaluated at the true parameter is asymptotically \(\chi^2_1\). An approximate 95% confidence set is therefore:

\(\displaystyle C_{\mathrm{LR}}(y)\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \left\{\theta:\ 2[\ell_n(\hat\theta)-\ell_n(\theta)]\leq\chi^2_{1,0.95}\right\}\)\(\approx\)\(\displaystyle \left\{\theta:\ 2[\ell_n(\hat\theta)-\ell_n(\theta)]\leq3.84\right\}\)

The endpoints occur where the log-likelihood has fallen far enough from its maximum to reach the cutoff. The resulting interval can be asymmetric and often reflects a skewed likelihood more faithfully than a symmetric Wald interval. Its usual chi-square calibration is still an asymptotic approximation.

Bootstrap

Estimate Uncertainty By Resampling

The bootstrap estimates sampling uncertainty by resampling and recomputing the estimator. The empirical distribution of the resulting estimates approximates its sampling distribution.

MethodProcedure
Nonparametric Bootstrap
  1. Resample the observed dataset with replacement, keeping the original sample size
  2. Recompute the estimator for each resample
  3. Use the distribution of bootstrap estimates to obtain a standard error, a percentile interval, and a bias estimate
Parametric Bootstrap
  1. Fit the statistical model
  2. Simulate new datasets of the same size from the fitted model
  3. Refit each simulated dataset to obtain a new estimate
  4. Build the empirical distribution of those estimates
  5. Use that distribution to obtain a standard error, a percentile interval, and a bias estimate

A bootstrap standard error is the standard deviation of the bootstrap estimates. A 95% percentile interval uses their 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. A bootstrap bias estimate compares their average with the original estimate.

Why bootstrap is useful

  • It does not rely as heavily on analytic formulas
  • It is useful when standard errors are difficult to derive
  • It can be useful for complicated estimators, including penalized or MAP estimators

Ordinary observation-by-observation resampling assumes independent observations. Bootstrap intervals are approximations and can also be unreliable in small samples or near parameter boundaries.

Uncertainty for MAP Estimates

Posterior Covariance And Sampling Variance

From a frequentist viewpoint, MAP is a penalized maximum-likelihood estimator. Its uncertainty can be studied in two distinct ways:

ViewpointUncertainty Calculation
Bayesian

Use the curvature of the log posterior at the MAP estimate:

\[\Sigma_{\mathrm{post}}\approx\left[-\left.\nabla^2_\theta\log p(\theta\mid y)\right|_{\theta=\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MAP}}}\right]^{-1}\]

Earlier derivations: MAP as a prior-regularized objective

This is an approximate posterior covariance, obtained through a local normal, or Laplace, approximation. It requires a smooth interior mode, positive-definite negative Hessian, and an adequately quadratic log posterior near that mode.

Frequentist

Use the bootstrap to approximate the sampling distribution of the MAP estimator, then extract its variance or a percentile interval. Refit the same estimation procedure, including the prior or penalty, in each bootstrap sample.

Posterior curvature measures posterior uncertainty about the parameter. It does not generally equal the frequentist sampling covariance of the MAP estimator. A posterior standard deviation and a sampling standard error describe different distributions.

Normal Mean with Known Variance

Example

25 Observations With Sample Mean 2

Model
25 independent normal observations, \(X_i\sim\mathcal N(\mu,1)\). The population variance is known and fixed at 1.
Parameters to estimate
The population mean \(\mu\). Compare the MLE and its sampling uncertainty with a Bayesian estimate and posterior uncertainty after introducing a prior.

Consider \(n=25\) independent observations from a normal distribution with known variance:

\[X_1,\ldots,X_{25}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\mathcal N(\mu,1)\]

Earlier derivations: Confidence interval with known population variance

We want to estimate the mean. The observed sample mean is \(\bar x=2\).

CalculationResult
01

MLE Point Estimate

\[\hat\mu_{\mathrm{MLE}}=\bar x=2.0\]
02

Fisher Information And Standard Error

\[I_n(\mu)=\frac{n}{\sigma^2}=25\]

The inverse Fisher information gives the Cramér–Rao lower bound on the variance of an unbiased estimator:

\[\operatorname{Var}(\hat\mu)\ \geq\ \frac{1}{I_n(\mu)}=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}=0.04\]

The sample mean attains this lower bound:

\(\displaystyle \operatorname{Var}(\hat\mu_{\mathrm{MLE}})\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \operatorname{Var}(\bar X)\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{\sigma^2}{n}=\frac{1}{25}=0.04\)
\[\operatorname{SE}(\hat\mu_{\mathrm{MLE}})=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{25}}=0.2\]
03

Wald 95% Confidence Interval

\[2.0\pm1.96(0.2)\]
\[C_{\mathrm{Wald}}=[1.608,\ 2.392]\]

Here the sample mean has an exact normal sampling distribution because the data are normal and the variance is known. Thus the normal interval is exact, apart from rounding the critical value to 1.96.

04

Likelihood-Ratio Interval

Evaluate the log-likelihood at candidate values of μ and compare it with its maximum to form the likelihood-ratio interval.

05

Bootstrap

  1. Resample the 25 observations with replacement
  2. Compute the sample mean for each resample
  3. Assemble the bootstrap distribution of the sample mean
  4. Evaluate its median and percentile interval

With 1,000 resamples, the example gives:

\[\text{Bootstrap median}=2.0\]
\[C_{\mathrm{bootstrap}}=[1.636,\ 2.361]\]

Include A Prior For The Mean

Now use a non-flat Gaussian prior for the mean:

\[\mu\sim\mathcal N(0,4)\]

The prior mean is 0 and its variance is 4. Combining this prior with the normal likelihood gives a normal posterior.

CalculationResult
01

Posterior Variance

\[v_{\mathrm{post}}=\frac{1}{25.25}\approx0.0396\]
02

Posterior And MAP Estimate

\[\mu\mid x\sim\mathcal N\!\left(\frac{50}{25.25},\frac{1}{25.25}\right)\]

A normal distribution has the same mean and mode, so:

\[\hat\mu_{\mathrm{MAP}}=m_{\mathrm{post}}\approx1.98\]
03

95% Credible Interval

\[\operatorname{SD}(\mu\mid x)=\sqrt{v_{\mathrm{post}}}\approx0.199\]
\[1.98\pm1.96(0.199)\approx[1.59,\ 2.37]\]

The normal example gives similar numerical intervals, but their interpretations remain different. The confidence interval describes repeated-sample coverage; the credible interval contains 95% of the posterior probability.

Derivation Normal Posterior Mean And Variance

Posterior precision is the sum of the data precision and the prior precision:

\(\displaystyle v_{\mathrm{post}}\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \left(\frac{n}{\sigma^2}+\frac{1}{4}\right)^{-1}\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \left(25+\frac{1}{4}\right)^{-1}\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{1}{25.25}\approx0.0396\)

The posterior mean weights the sample mean and prior mean by their precisions:

\(\displaystyle m_{\mathrm{post}}\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle v_{\mathrm{post}}\left(\frac{n\bar x}{\sigma^2}+\frac{0}{4}\right)\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{25(2)+0}{25.25}\)\(\approx\)\(\displaystyle 1.9802\)

Coin-Flip Probability

Example

2 Heads In 20 Trials

Model
20 independent Bernoulli flips with head probability \(p\); equivalently the head count follows \(K\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(20,p)\).
Parameters to estimate
The head probability \(p\in[0,1]\). Compare point estimates, frequentist confidence intervals, and a posterior credible interval after introducing a prior.

A coin has unknown head probability \(p\). We observe 2 heads in 20 independent trials.

CalculationResult
01

MLE Point Estimate

\[\hat p_{\mathrm{MLE}}=\frac{2}{20}=0.1\]
02

Wald Approximation

The estimated standard error is:

\(\displaystyle \widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat p)\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}}\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \sqrt{\frac{0.1\cdot0.9}{20}}\)\(\approx\)\(\displaystyle 0.0671\)

The 95% Wald interval is:

\[0.1\pm1.96(0.0671)\approx0.1\pm0.131\]
\[C_{\mathrm{Wald}}\approx[-0.031,\ 0.231]\]

The lower endpoint is outside the allowable probability range. This indicates that the normal approximation is poor in this small-sample, near-boundary setting.

03

Likelihood-Ratio Interval

\[2[\ell(\hat p)-\ell(p)]\leq3.84\]
\[C_{\mathrm{LR}}\approx[0.017,\ 0.278]\]

The asymmetric interval reflects the skewness of the likelihood more closely than the symmetric Wald interval. The chi-square cutoff still provides approximate coverage.

04

Bootstrap Interval

A simple nonparametric bootstrap percentile interval is approximately:

\[C_{\mathrm{bootstrap}}\approx[0,\ 0.25]\]

This interval is also asymmetric about the observed estimate. Its endpoints depend on the discrete bootstrap distribution, and a finite resampling run can introduce additional variation.

Include A Uniform Prior

Use a uniform prior on the probability \(p\):

\[p\sim\operatorname{Beta}(1,1)\]

After observing 2 heads and 18 tails, the posterior is:

\[p\mid x\sim\operatorname{Beta}(1+2,\ 1+18)=\operatorname{Beta}(3,19)\]
CalculationResult
01

MAP Point Estimate

\(\displaystyle \hat p_{\mathrm{MAP}}\)
\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{3-1}{3+19-2}\)\(=\)\(\displaystyle \frac{2}{20}=0.1\)
02

95% Posterior Credible Interval

Using the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the \(\operatorname{Beta}(3,19)\) posterior:

\[C_{\mathrm{credible}}\approx[0.030,\ 0.304]\]

With a skewed likelihood and few observed heads, the intervals differ substantially across methods. The Wald interval is a poor approximation here. The credible interval makes a posterior probability statement, while the frequentist intervals aim for repeated-sample coverage.
